n: These are David’s “last words” — perhaps his final poetic testimony. He describes himself as a shepherd’s son raised high by God, anointed king, and Israel’s beloved singer of psalms.

f.g: Or “the favorite of the songs of Israel” — the one Israel loved to sing about, or Israel’s pleasant singer.

n: David testifies that his words came by inspiration: the Spirit of the Lord spoke through him. Jesus and the apostles also taught that David spoke by the Holy Ghost.

f.w: The Spirit of the LORD spake by me

n: God’s message to him concerns the ideal ruler: one who governs justly and in reverence for God.

f.w: He that ruleth over men must be just

f.g: Reverent awe and obedience toward God.

n: Such a ruler is like a cloudless sunrise, or like fresh grass sparkling after rain — bringing life and blessing to his people. Christians see the perfect fulfillment in Jesus Christ.

f.w: as the light of the morning
the tender grass springing out of the earth

n: David admits his own house has not always been righteous, yet God has made an everlasting covenant with him, secure in every detail. This covenant is his whole hope.

f.w: ordered in all things, and sure
f.g: Carefully arranged and guaranteed.

f.w: although he make it not to grow
f.g: The Hebrew can also be read as a question: “Will He not make it grow?” — an expression of confidence.

n: In contrast, the wicked are like thorns that are thrown away — too prickly to grab with bare hands.

f.g: Worthless, wicked people.

n: Thorns are handled with iron tools and burned up on the spot — a picture of how evildoers will finally be removed.

f.g: Armed, equipped.

n: The chapter now honors David’s elite warriors. First is Josheb-basshebeth (called the Tachmonite and Adino), the chief of the Three, who killed eight hundred in one fight.

f.w: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat
f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; 1 Chronicles 11:11 names him Jashobeam the Hachmonite.
Chronicles gives 300.

n: Second of the Three is Eleazar, who stood with David against the Philistines when Israel’s army retreated.
He fought until his hand cramped and stuck to his sword. The narrator credits the Lord for the victory; the rest of the army came back only to collect the spoil.

f.w: his hand clave unto the sword
f.g: Clave = stuck; his grip had frozen from exhaustion.

f.w: the LORD wrought a great victory

n: Third is Shammah. When the people fled from the Philistines in a lentil field, he did not.

f.g: Possibly “the mountaineer,” from the hill country.
A field of lentils — food for the people.

n: He stood his ground alone in the middle of the field and defended it. Again, the Lord gave the victory. Sometimes faithfulness means holding firm where you are.

f.w: he stood in the midst of the ground

n: A story from David’s early outlaw days: three of the Thirty come to him at the cave of Adullam while the Philistines occupy the valley near Jerusalem.
David is in his stronghold, and a Philistine garrison holds his hometown of Bethlehem.

f.g: A stronghold or fortress.

n: Homesick, David wishes aloud for a drink from the well by Bethlehem’s gate, the water of his childhood.

f.g: Perhaps a cistern near the town gate.

n: His three warriors break through enemy lines and bring him the water. But David refuses to drink it and pours it out as an offering to the Lord.

f.w: poured it out unto the LORD
f.g: A drink offering — giving to God something too precious to keep for oneself.

n: David says drinking it would be like drinking the blood of men who risked their lives. He honors their sacrifice by giving it to God. Their loyalty and his reverence both shine here.

f.w: the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives
f.g: Jeopardy = danger.

n: Abishai, Joab’s brother, led another group of three and once killed three hundred men with his spear.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “chief of the thirty.”

n: He was honored and became their commander, though he did not rank with the first Three.

f.g: Did not equal; did not reach the rank of.

n: Benaiah, a valiant man from Kabzeel in southern Judah, did many deeds: he killed two of Moab’s great warriors and, on a snowy day, killed a lion in a pit.

f.g: The Hebrew ’ari’el is unclear: great champions, or perhaps “the two sons of Ariel.”

n: He also faced a huge Egyptian armed with a spear, using only a club. He snatched the spear and killed the man with his own weapon — echoing David’s defeat of Goliath.

f.g: An impressive, large man; 1 Chronicles 11:23 says he was five cubits (about 7.5 feet) tall.

f.w: slew him with his own spear

n: These deeds made Benaiah famous alongside the Three.
Benaiah was honored above the Thirty, though not among the Three. David made him commander of his personal bodyguard; he later became Solomon’s army commander.
The roster of the Thirty begins. Asahel heads the list, though he died early in David’s reign — a mark of honor. Elhanan of Bethlehem was from David’s hometown.

f.g: A different man from the Elhanan in 2 Samuel 21:19.

n: Two warriors from Harod, perhaps near the spring where Gideon chose his three hundred.

f.g: From Harod, possibly a town in Judah or near the spring of Harod.

n: Helez came from Beth-pelet in southern Judah, and Ira from Tekoa — the hometown of the wise woman and, later, of Amos.
Abiezer came from Anathoth, a priestly town in Benjamin that would later be Jeremiah’s home. Mebunnai came from Hushah in Judah.

f.g: Likely the same man as Sibbechai the Hushathite; the names look alike in Hebrew.

n: Zalmon was of the Ahohite clan, like Eleazar of the Three. Maharai came from Netophah, a village near Bethlehem.

f.g: From Netophah, close to Bethlehem.

n: Heleb was another Netophathite. This Ittai (not the Philistine Ittai) was from Gibeah of Benjamin — Saul’s own hometown, showing that some Benjaminites were loyal to David.

f.g: Different from Ittai the Gittite in 2 Samuel 15:19.

f.w: Gibeah of the children of Benjamin

n: This Benaiah came from Pirathon in Ephraim, the hometown of the judge Abdon. Hiddai came from the ravines of Mount Gaash, near Joshua’s burial place.
Abi-albon was from Beth-arabah near the Jordan valley; Azmaveth from Bahurim, the village of Shimei.

f.g: Probably from Bahurim (2 Samuel 16:5), with two letters reversed.

n: Eliahba came from Shaalbim, a town once held by the Amorites. The sons of Jashen and Jonathan follow.

f.g: From Shaalbim, in the territory of Dan.

n: Shammah the Hararite (perhaps the father of Jonathan) and Ahiam come from the hill country.

f.g: Perhaps related to the Shammah of the Three, or the same man.

n: Eliphelet’s family came from Maacah, an Aramean region. Eliam, son of Ahithophel, may be the father of Bath-sheba — which would make the betrayal of her husband and the later rebellion of her grandfather all the more tangled.
Hezrai came from Carmel in Judah, the home of Nabal and Abigail; Paarai from Arab, another town in Judah’s hill country.
Igal came from Zobah, an Aramean kingdom David had defeated, and Bani from the tribe of Gad east of the Jordan. David’s army included former enemies.
Zelek was an Ammonite, and Naharai came from Beeroth — the town of Ish-bosheth’s murderers. He served as Joab’s armor-bearer.
Ira and Gareb were Ithrites, a clan from the area of Kirjath-jearim, where the ark had once rested.

The list ends with a sobering name: Uriah the Hittite, the loyal warrior David betrayed. Placing him last makes readers remember David’s sin even while honoring his heroes. The total of thirty-seven includes the leaders named earlier.

f.g: The Thirty plus the Three, Abishai, Benaiah, and probably Joab as commander.
